newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan stocks seen rising in third quarter 1997.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan stocks seen rising in third quarter 1997.

text.p: Pakistan stocks are unlikely to experience a sustained recovery before an expected economic up-turn in the third quarter of 1997, analysts said on Tuesday.

"Fundamentally, the market is even attractive at current levels. What it lacks is improved liquidity, investor confidence and more depth," Anisur Rehman, head of research at SocGen-Crosby Securities, told Reuters. "All these factors are expected to improve by third quarter 1997."
Analysts said they expected a turn-around in September when the International Monetary Fund is expected to announce the reinstatement of a huge loan to Pakistan.

The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index surged to a nine-month high of 1,775.57 on February 20 from 1,353.34 on January 1 amid a bull run prompted by the crushing victory of pro-business politician Nawaz Sharif in February 3 general elections.
But the sentiment-driven rally has since run out of steam, slipping below the 1,600-point barrier on March 6.
Many investors, aware that the economy was still in the doldrums with a deteriorating external sector, took the rise above 1,700 points as an exit opportunity, analysts said.

Rehman said a three-year decline since the market peaked at 2,661 in March 1994 had placed local institutions in a cash crunch, while most foreign investors were holding investments which could not be liquidated due to bearish conditions.
"In 1996, the market twice crossed 1,750 only to correct sharply due to selling by local institutions," he said.
Analysts say the Pakistan bourse, currently the cheapest in Asia, offers high growth at low multiples, but only if the economic numbers improve, particularly on the external front.
"Pakistan has been meeting its debt-servicing requirements mostly through borrowings at very high cost and faces a severe mismatch of loan repayments," Rehman said.
With liquid reserves of just over $1.0 billion Pakistan faces debt payments totalling an estimated $1.6 billion during the March-June period, bankers say.
"We expect the divergent trends between a strengthening domestic economic scene and a volatile external payment situation to persist until mid-1997," Rehman said.
After that, the new government will be able to show the market, along with international lenders and donors, that it can keep its commitments under a restructuring programme, he said.

"We expect a turning point in September when it is very likely that the IMF will announce the reinstatement of the $1.5 billion ESAF (Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility) loan to Pakistan," he said.
An IMF mission is currently in Islamabad to review the economy and decide whether to recommend release of the next $122 million tranche of a standby loan, due by the end of March.
Investors are keenly awaiting the outcome, which will signal whether Pakistan's new government is in harmony with the IMF.
Kalim Aziz, research head at ING Baring Securities, said IMF backing could transform Pakistan's prospects.

"With the new pro-business government in place, improved market sentiment and general level of confidence a significant improvement in economic growth from a low of five percent to as high as seven percent is not an unlikely scenario," he said.
Given IMF approval, his firm's call would be a buy at 1,850 points and a sell initially at levels above 2,300.
Rehman said a positive budget in June, speedy privatisation and resumption of an ESAF programme would turn the economy round and stimulate foreign investors to jump back into the market.
